news.title: Trump 'gleefully eviscerating' efforts to help families with 'illegal' move: Dem senator
news.description: Elected Democrats—and even the Senate’s top Republican appropriator—blasted President Donald Trump late Friday for rescinding nearly $1 billion in congressionally approved spending that the White House deemed “wasteful and harmful” through a legally contested process. In a statement announcing what was targeted, the administration celebrated funding cuts for what it called “pro-illegal immigration programs,” a “nefarious” Department of Justice subagency, a program that “propagates America Last climate alarmism,” an office that promotes diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI)—or “discrimination, and radical woke ideologies”—and more. House Budget Committee Ranking Member Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.) responded in a statement that “ Donald Trump knows he can’t get these cuts through Congress, so he is illegally making them through the back door.” “Trump’s actions are a blatant attack on Congress’ constitutional power of the purse,” he added. “It is exactly why we need to pass my Congressional Power of the Purse Act and stop any president from illegally overriding Congress.” The Associated Press reported that “under federal law, Congress has 45 days to review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year and the House out of session through the November election.” Senate Budget Committee Ranking Member Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) stressed on social media that “a pocket rescission is an illegal line-item veto. It is the president saying that he and he alone will convert a bipartisan spending bill (that has been signed into law) into a partisan spending bill. He is canceling the lines of spending he doesn’t like.” “This violates the core separation of powers embedded in our Constitution in which it is the Congress, not the president, who decides what programs are designed and at what level they are funded,” he continued. “Republican colleagues said they would never let this happen. Well, here it is. They should ask themselves: ‘How would I like to have a Democratic president canceling out the Republican flavored programs he or she doesn’t like in a bipartisan spending bill that has been signed into law?’ If they have any integrity or any spine, they will join us in ending this practice.” Noting that the cuts will impact everything from critical health research , to combating the international illicit narcotics trade , Senate Appropriations Committee Vice Chair Patty Murray (D-Wash.) declared : “This is theft from the American people, plain and simple. These are funds Congress has delivered on a bipartisan basis and should be helping people—not cut off by a president more focused on building a ballroom than investing in families.” She specifically called out Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought—a co-author of Project 2025 , the Heritage Foundation-led blueprint for a right-wing overhaul of the federal government, who was recently condemned as an “unelected shadow president” by the House Democrat who introduced impeachment articles against him. According to Murray, “Every Republican who voted for these bills should be furious because Vought is saying their votes don’t count.” Murray also pointed out that during negotiations for the recently enacted stopgap spending legislation, “Democrats fought to include language to prevent the Trump administration from once again usurping Congress’ power—but for the second time in a year, Republicans refused to take common sense action and prevent this from happening.” “While Trump spends tax dollars on ads promoting himself, Congress needs to reassert its powers to help people, and it’s past time Republicans join us in that fight,” she argued. “Russ Vought’s message to Congress is that your votes don’t count, and your laws are optional. It is now time for my Republican colleagues who said they would never let this happen to stand up and join us to stop this, and remind this administration this is not how this works.” A rescission requires an act of Congress. This? It’s an illegal impoundment. https://t.co/UDAlMQ3zkI — Bobby Kogan (@BBKogan) September 26, 2026 Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) emphasized the impact of the administration’s move, saying that “Trump is gleefully eviscerating programs and protections that help hardworking American families live a safe and healthy life, all while he continues to punish them with skyrocketing gas and grocery prices.” “With this rescissions package, the Trump administration is illegally stripping nearly $1 billion in critical funding that supports kids, K-12 students, small businesses, and health and clean air research,” he highlighted. “Americans are crying out for relief.” “Instead of ending his Iran War and tariff chaos that are driving up costs, Trump is rolling out the red carpet for our adversaries while stealing funds meant to help American families,” he added. “Senate Democrats will challenge Trump’s illegal cuts at every turn and continue the fight to help American families, lower healthcare costs and secure our communities.” The administration’s rescission announcement came less than six weeks away from the midterm elections . Democrats aim to win majorities, while Trump’s Republican Party is fighting to keep control of both chambers of Congress. One of the nationally watched races is that of Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine). As some congressional Republicans cheered the Friday action, Collins put out a statement denouncing it. She said that “without warning or consultation, Congress just received an $810 million package of pocket rescissions from the administration,” which she called OMB's most recent attempt “to undermine Congress’ constitutional power of the purse.” “This move shows that OMB intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation of appropriations that were approved on a bipartisan basis and signed into law,” Collins continued. “Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’ appropriations powers. OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.” “The independent Government Accountability Office has concluded that pocket rescissions are unlawful and not permitted by the Impoundment Control Act,” she added. “Any effort to rescind appropriated funds without congressional approval is a clear violation of the law. I will work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions.” YOU literally voted to confirm Trump’s OMB Director, Russ Vought, who has always wanted to usurp Congress’ authority over spending. https://t.co/RhgSqk6z8O — Jordan Wood (@JordanWood) September 26, 2026 While some Democrats had called for their Republican colleagues to make such promises, Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) fired back at Collins on social media, writing that “Senate Republicans had chance after chance to stop Trump’s illegal seizure of taxpayer money. Time after time, they pledged allegiance to Trump instead of to citizens. And he’ll keep rolling them if the Senate doesn’t change hands.” So did Troy Jackson, the former Democratic Maine Senate president running to unseat Collins. He said that “Susan Collins voted for Trump’s pick to lead the OMB. Now she’s surprised he’s doing exactly what he promised to do? She’s the appropriations chair who voted with Trump 96% of the time. Expressing concern isn’t enough. Mainers see through the bull----.”

news.title: The Senate map is shifting toward Democrats, with new openings in red states
news.description: Democrats’ chances of flipping the Senate have grown in recent months as President Donald Trump’s unpopularity, as well as frustration with the economy, push voters away from Republicans. Democrats have been favored to seize control of the House, which has a narrow Republican majority. The math in the Senate is more daunting: Democrats control 47 seats to Republicans’ 53. Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post. The clearest path to a majority requires Democrats to retain all of their seats and win four GOP-controlled seats, including at least two in states President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024. That path, which once felt like a long shot, now seems feasible. A Wednesday update from the Cook Political Report, a nonpartisan election analysis site, described control of the Senate as “a true coin flip, with viable paths for both parties to win or keep a majority.” Some other analysts have concluded the map is even more favorable to Democrats. The political environment has shifted enough in recent months that some Republicans have suggested that the GOP should scale back spending in Georgia and North Carolina, where Trump won in 2024 but the party’s nominees have lagged in polls. Here are the races to watch as the battle for the Senate grows increasingly competitive. The races moving toward Democrats: Georgia, Iowa, Texas, Kansas, South Carolina Sen. Jon Ossoff is now heavily favored to win reelection in Georgia in a race which Cook rates as “Likely Democratic.” Republicans initially viewed the race as one of their leading opportunities to gain a seat, but controversies involving the GOP nominee, Rep. Mike Collins, have helped Ossoff pull away. Iowa and Texas, two states that backed Trump by a double-digit margin in 2024, are now in the toss-up column. James Talarico, a state representative, has led Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in many polls as he tries to become the first Democrat to win a statewide election in Texas this century. After Paxton defeated Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary, the race exploded into an expensive, high-profile contest. Scandals have eroded Paxton’s popularity, while Democrats hope that Talarico’s faith-based politics has broad appeal and can overcome criticism that he’s too socially liberal. Josh Turek, an Iowa state representative and former Paralympic athlete, is tapping voters’ frustrations with the effects of Trump’s tariffs to try to win crossover support. He faces Rep. Ashley Hinson, a former television anchor viewed by national Republicans as a strong candidate, for the seat being vacated by retiring Republican Joni Ernst. Kansas, a state which Trump won by 16 percentage points in 2024, has emerged as a surprising Democratic target in recent months. Although incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall is still favored, the challenge from Adam Hamilton, a political outsider and prominent pastor, has concerned some Republicans. In South Carolina, Republican Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed after her brother, Lindsey Graham, died in July, is favored to defeat Democratic pediatrician Annie Andrews. Graham’s weaknesses include a lack of political experience and skepticism about her right-wing credentials from some conservatives who preferred her opponents in the Republican primary. The one race shifting toward Republicans: New Hampshire New Hampshire, a state Kamala Harris won in 2024, is one of Republicans’ best chances of flipping a Democratic seat. Polls have shown a close race between Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas and Republican John Sununu, who served in the Senate from 2003 to 2009 and is the son of former governor John H. Sununu and brother to popular former governor Chris Sununu. They are competing to succeed retiring Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D). Republicans plan to spend heavily in the state to support Sununu, who has distanced himself from Trump. The other battlegrounds: North Carolina, Alaska, Maine, Michigan, Ohio Michigan’s race presents another opportunity for Republicans to flip a Democratic-controlled seat, as Republicans have criticized the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, as being too far to the left. El-Sayed has sought to unify Michigan Democrats since winning a bruising primary against Rep. Haley Stevens. A recent Washington Post-Schar School poll showed him with a narrow edge but lagging the Democratic nominee for governor among Black voters, independents and voters who say they are unwilling to support a Muslim for president. Republicans describe their nominee, former eight-term congressman Mike Rogers, as a formidable candidate who narrowly lost a 2024 campaign for Senate. Democrats have sought to tie him to Trump, whose popularity remains low in the state. In North Carolina, Gov. Roy Cooper, a popular Democrat, is favored over former Republican National Committee chair Michael Whatley in a race that looks to be Democrats’ likeliest flip. The swing state’s race has been a top target of Democrats since incumbent Sen. Thom Tillis (R) announced his retirement in 2025. Both parties have spent heavily on the race, but Cooper has consistently led in public polling. In Alaska, Democrats are hopeful that former congresswoman Mary Peltola, a moderate, can oust Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R). Peltola’s path to victory in the deep red state might rely upon frustration with high diesel prices and the presence of three other Republicans, including retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, on the state’s ranked-choice election ballot. Maine’s race has undergone a significant shake-up in recent months after former nominee Graham Platner withdrew following an allegation of sexual assault. Troy Jackson, a progressive logger and former state Senate president who was nominated to replace Platner at a convention, is hoping to unseat longtime Sen. Susan Collins (R), who has long cultivated a moderate image to garner crossover support. In Ohio, former longtime senator Sherrod Brown (D) faces Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed in 2025 after his predecessor, JD Vance, became vice president. Although Brown lost reelection by four percentage points in 2024 while Trump won the state by a double-digit margin, analysts believe that Trump’s lagging popularity could fuel Brown’s comeback. The reach states: Minnesota and Nebraska Cook rates Democrats and Republicans, respectively, as “likely” to hold their seats in Minnesota and Nebraska, but their victories are not assured. In Nebraska, independent Dan Osborn, a union leader who says he would not caucus with either Democrats or Republicans in the Senate, faces Sen. Pete Ricketts (R), the son of billionaire TD Ameritrade founder Joe Ricketts. Osborn ran for Senate in 2024 and overperformed in losing by seven percentage points while Trump won by 20 percentage points. Democrats are not fielding a candidate, and the state party endorsed Osborn. Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan (D) faces former football journalist Michele Tafoya, a Republican, in a state Harris won by four percentage points. Flanagan defeated a more moderate candidate in a bruising primary. Republicans hope that voters unhappy with the outgoing Democratic governor, Tim Walz, will punish Flanagan and that Tafoya will benefit from her high-profile career as a sideline reporter. CORRECTION: A previous version of this article incorrectly said that Republican Mike Rogers outperformed Donald Trump when he narrowly lost the Michigan Senate race in 2024. Trump won Michigan in the presidential election that year. Theodoric Meyer contributed reporting to this article. - - - Graphics: Shift in Senate race ratings Related Content This article originally appeared on Washington Post at https://washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/09/26/democratic-senate-is-becoming-more-likely-here-are-races-watch/

news.title: Trump 'gleefully eviscerating' efforts to help families with 'illegal' move: Dem senator
news.description: Elected Democrats—and even the Senate’s top Republican appropriator—blasted President Donald Trump late Friday for rescinding nearly $1 billion in congressionally approved spending that the White House deemed “wasteful and harmful” through a legally contested process. In a statement announcing what was targeted, the administration celebrated funding cuts for what it called “pro-illegal immigration programs,” a “nefarious” Department of Justice subagency, a program that “propagates America Last climate alarmism,” an office that promotes diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI)—or “discrimination, and radical woke ideologies”—and more. House Budget Committee Ranking Member Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.) responded in a statement that “ Donald Trump knows he can’t get these cuts through Congress, so he is illegally making them through the back door.” “Trump’s actions are a blatant attack on Congress’ constitutional power of the purse,” he added. “It is exactly why we need to pass my Congressional Power of the Purse Act and stop any president from illegally overriding Congress.” The Associated Press reported that “under federal law, Congress has 45 days to review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year and the House out of session through the November election.” Senate Budget Committee Ranking Member Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) stressed on social media that “a pocket rescission is an illegal line-item veto. It is the president saying that he and he alone will convert a bipartisan spending bill (that has been signed into law) into a partisan spending bill. He is canceling the lines of spending he doesn’t like.” “This violates the core separation of powers embedded in our Constitution in which it is the Congress, not the president, who decides what programs are designed and at what level they are funded,” he continued. “Republican colleagues said they would never let this happen. Well, here it is. They should ask themselves: ‘How would I like to have a Democratic president canceling out the Republican flavored programs he or she doesn’t like in a bipartisan spending bill that has been signed into law?’ If they have any integrity or any spine, they will join us in ending this practice.” Noting that the cuts will impact everything from critical health research , to combating the international illicit narcotics trade , Senate Appropriations Committee Vice Chair Patty Murray (D-Wash.) declared : “This is theft from the American people, plain and simple. These are funds Congress has delivered on a bipartisan basis and should be helping people—not cut off by a president more focused on building a ballroom than investing in families.” She specifically called out Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought—a co-author of Project 2025 , the Heritage Foundation-led blueprint for a right-wing overhaul of the federal government, who was recently condemned as an “unelected shadow president” by the House Democrat who introduced impeachment articles against him. According to Murray, “Every Republican who voted for these bills should be furious because Vought is saying their votes don’t count.” Murray also pointed out that during negotiations for the recently enacted stopgap spending legislation, “Democrats fought to include language to prevent the Trump administration from once again usurping Congress’ power—but for the second time in a year, Republicans refused to take common sense action and prevent this from happening.” “While Trump spends tax dollars on ads promoting himself, Congress needs to reassert its powers to help people, and it’s past time Republicans join us in that fight,” she argued. “Russ Vought’s message to Congress is that your votes don’t count, and your laws are optional. It is now time for my Republican colleagues who said they would never let this happen to stand up and join us to stop this, and remind this administration this is not how this works.” A rescission requires an act of Congress. This? It’s an illegal impoundment. https://t.co/UDAlMQ3zkI — Bobby Kogan (@BBKogan) September 26, 2026 Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) emphasized the impact of the administration’s move, saying that “Trump is gleefully eviscerating programs and protections that help hardworking American families live a safe and healthy life, all while he continues to punish them with skyrocketing gas and grocery prices.” “With this rescissions package, the Trump administration is illegally stripping nearly $1 billion in critical funding that supports kids, K-12 students, small businesses, and health and clean air research,” he highlighted. “Americans are crying out for relief.” “Instead of ending his Iran War and tariff chaos that are driving up costs, Trump is rolling out the red carpet for our adversaries while stealing funds meant to help American families,” he added. “Senate Democrats will challenge Trump’s illegal cuts at every turn and continue the fight to help American families, lower healthcare costs and secure our communities.” The administration’s rescission announcement came less than six weeks away from the midterm elections . Democrats aim to win majorities, while Trump’s Republican Party is fighting to keep control of both chambers of Congress. One of the nationally watched races is that of Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine). As some congressional Republicans cheered the Friday action, Collins put out a statement denouncing it. She said that “without warning or consultation, Congress just received an $810 million package of pocket rescissions from the administration,” which she called OMB's most recent attempt “to undermine Congress’ constitutional power of the purse.” “This move shows that OMB intentionally withheld these funds for months to execute this unlawful cancellation of appropriations that were approved on a bipartisan basis and signed into law,” Collins continued. “Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’ appropriations powers. OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.” “The independent Government Accountability Office has concluded that pocket rescissions are unlawful and not permitted by the Impoundment Control Act,” she added. “Any effort to rescind appropriated funds without congressional approval is a clear violation of the law. I will work with my colleagues to address these illegal actions.” YOU literally voted to confirm Trump’s OMB Director, Russ Vought, who has always wanted to usurp Congress’ authority over spending. https://t.co/RhgSqk6z8O — Jordan Wood (@JordanWood) September 26, 2026 While some Democrats had called for their Republican colleagues to make such promises, Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) fired back at Collins on social media, writing that “Senate Republicans had chance after chance to stop Trump’s illegal seizure of taxpayer money. Time after time, they pledged allegiance to Trump instead of to citizens. And he’ll keep rolling them if the Senate doesn’t change hands.” So did Troy Jackson, the former Democratic Maine Senate president running to unseat Collins. He said that “Susan Collins voted for Trump’s pick to lead the OMB. Now she’s surprised he’s doing exactly what he promised to do? She’s the appropriations chair who voted with Trump 96% of the time. Expressing concern isn’t enough. Mainers see through the bull----.”
